railTransportProduct.name: Rail Transport as a Tourism Product

flashcards.question: In which ways is the railway applied IN TOURISM (rail as a tourism product)?
flashcards.explanation: Even when attractive, rail rarely works alone — it usually needs road transport for the door-to-door part.

flashcards.question: What are TOURIST TRAINS (occasional/line system)?
flashcards.answer:
Trains to which special carriages are added — catering, overnight (sleeping) and PASSENGER-CAR transport. Tourist trains connect places over long distances with strong, constant SEASONAL tourist flows.

Car-carrying wagons let tourists keep their own car at the destination — which also reduces the volume of road traffic.
flashcards.explanation: A neat sustainability bonus: putting cars on trains for the long haul cuts road congestion and emissions.

flashcards.question: What is RAILWAY TOURISM (multi-day train journeys)? Give the two styles.
flashcards.answer:
Railway tourism = the train trip itself is the holiday — the transport service DOMINATES the product.

Two styles:
• HISTORICAL / luxury (the Venice Simplon-Orient-Express) — luxury, comfort, fine dining;
• MODERN, landscape-focused (the Rocky Mountaineer) — panoramic coaches, regional cuisine, storytelling, daytime-only with luxury-hotel overnights.
Journeys can cross thousands of km and last 10+ days; have a LINE character.
flashcards.explanation: Here transport is the backbone of the tourist offer — the opposite of rail as a mere connector.

flashcards.question: What is PANORAMIC rail transport in a limited destination area?
flashcards.answer:
Short, closed rail systems in protected nature, amusement parks, caves and destinations, combining high ecological standards with tourism.

Differences from public rail: closed systems of shorter length; non-standard train dimensions; lower speed; capacity & appearance adapted to tourist demand.
flashcards.explanation: Designed for sightseeing inside a destination, not for transport between markets.

flashcards.question: What are railway EXCURSIONS (occasional transport)?
flashcards.explanation: Excursions reuse otherwise obsolete lines for tourism value.

flashcards.question: What are MOUNTAIN RAILWAYS, and how do they relate to FUNICULARS/cable cars?
flashcards.answer:
A MOUNTAIN RAILWAY operates in mountainous terrain — following valleys/tunnels or climbing to a summit; often NARROW-GAUGE for tight curves and lower cost. On steep gradients they use steep-grade technology or operate as FUNICULAR railways.

• FUNICULAR — a cable-hauled railway on rails where two cars counterbalance each other up/down a slope.
• CABLE CAR / aerial cableway — cabins suspended from a cable (no rails) to reach summits/viewpoints.
flashcards.explanation: Funicular & cable-car transport is explicitly a week-7 topic; both are classic destination attractions in mountain/scenic tourism.

flashcards.question: What does the EU survey say about SATISFACTION with passenger rail services?
flashcards.answer:
Most respondents are OCCASIONAL rail travellers (~67%); ~13% frequent, ~20% never. Top trip purpose: other leisure (~35%) and holidays (~23%).

Satisfaction is HIGH for buying tickets (~75%) and timetable information (~74%); lower for WiFi (~41%) and complaint handling (~38%). Most common reason for NOT travelling by train: difficulty getting to the station (~16%). Central/northern/western Europeans are most satisfied.
flashcards.explanation: Many rail trips are INTERMODAL — ~44% reach the station by car/motorbike/taxi.

quiz.question: Car-carrying wagons on tourist trains are valuable because they:
options: Let tourists keep their own car at the destination AND reduce road traffic

quiz.question: In 'railway tourism' (multi-day luxury/scenic trains), the transport service is:
options: The dominant backbone of the tourism product

quiz.question: The Venice Simplon-Orient-Express represents which style of railway tourism?
A funicular is best described as:
options: A cable-hauled rail vehicle with two counterbalanced cars on a slope

quiz.question: Panoramic rail transport in a destination differs from public rail by being:
options: Closed, shorter, slower, with non-standard trains adapted to tourist demand

quiz.question: Railway excursions often add tourism value by:
options: Valorising old/obsolete low-speed railways for sightseeing

quiz.question: In the EU rail survey, the most common reason for NOT travelling by train is:

fillBlanks.sentence: Trains with catering, sleeping and car-carrying wagons serving seasonal flows are _______ trains.
When the train journey itself is the holiday, we speak of railway _______.
A cable-hauled rail vehicle with two counterbalanced cars on a slope is a _______.
A _______ car uses cabins suspended from a cable (no rails) to reach viewpoints.
Mountain railways often use _______-gauge tracks to allow tight curves and lower cost.
Excursion, party and Christmas trains are forms of _______ rail transport.
About two-thirds of EU respondents are _______ rail travellers (less than once a week).

learn.title: Rail Transport in the Form of a Tourism Product
learn.content:
From connector to attraction

When the rail service stops being a mere connector and becomes the experience, rail turns into a tourism product. It still rarely works alone — road transport usually completes the door-to-door chain.

Rail in tourism: hub→destination links · tourist trains (car-carrying) · railway tourism (multi-day) · panoramic (in-destination) · excursions · mountain railways · funicular & cable car

The products

  • Tourist trains — add catering, sleeping & car-carrying wagons; serve seasonal flows and cut road traffic.
  • Railway tourism (multi-day) — the ride is the holiday; historical/luxury (Orient-Express) vs modern/scenic (Rocky Mountaineer).
  • Panoramic in-destination rail (parks, caves) & excursions (often reusing old lines).
  • Mountain railways (narrow-gauge, steep-grade) → funiculars (counterbalanced cars on rails) & cable cars (cabins on a cable) — classic scenic attractions.

What rail passengers think

~67% are occasional travellers; satisfaction is high for ticket-buying (~75%) & information (~74%), low for WiFi (~41%) & complaints (~38%); the top reason for NOT using trains is difficulty getting to the station (~16%) — which is why ~44% reach stations by car/taxi (intermodality).

flashcards.question: What are the ADVANTAGES of air transport?
flashcards.explanation: Air's unique selling point: speed over long/intercontinental distances no other mode can match.

flashcards.question: What are the DISADVANTAGES of air transport?
flashcards.explanation: The airport-transfer problem means a short/medium flight can take less time than getting to/from the airport.

flashcards.question: Is air traffic only AIRPLANE traffic?
flashcards.explanation: Identifying air traffic only with airplanes does not fully reflect reality, though airplanes dominate.

flashcards.question: Describe air transport INFRASTRUCTURE (the airport).
flashcards.answer:
Infrastructure is needed only at start/end points — AIRPORTS, which are complex multimodal hubs including: runways; manoeuvring areas; aircraft resting areas; flight-safety objects/devices; aircraft-service devices; passenger & cargo reception facilities; surfaces for other modes; access roads.

By purpose: local, national, international airports. Very expensive → built by state/local authorities/airlines.
flashcards.explanation: Airports are located near big cities (the source of demand) but far enough out that the transfer is a real issue.

flashcards.question: Within COMMERCIAL air traffic, contrast LINE (scheduled) carriers — traditional vs LOW-COST.
flashcards.answer:
Line carriers publish a flight schedule and must maintain routes/frequencies. Two camps:
• LARGE TRADITIONAL airlines — long-term dominance, government support, complex systems, agencies, big airports;
• LOW-COST carriers (LCC) — cut prices by: no free food/drinks, max passenger numbers, opening new markets/connecting smaller cities, several flights/day, fast turnarounds, SECONDARY airports, direct online ticket sales, fluctuating (dynamic) prices.
LCC ≠ charter! LCC carry ~30% of ~9 bn annual air passengers.
flashcards.explanation: By choosing small airports, LCC bring tourists to areas outside main streams and create NEW destinations.

flashcards.question: What is CHARTER air transport, and what are its TYPES?
flashcards.answer:
Charter = based on higher aircraft occupancy (80–90%) on high-demand routes, at LOWER service quality & price; needs a CONTRACT between airline (transport function) and travel agency (sales function).

TYPES: (1) WHOLE charter (entire aircraft); (2) PART/split charter (capacity split among agencies); (3) AD HOC (one transport); (4) SERIES (several consecutive); (5) TIME charter (exclusive use for the whole season — most rational/economical).
flashcards.explanation: Charter emerged in the 1950s with the surge of tourist flows; it is the classic 'package-holiday' flight.

flashcards.question: Beyond scheduled & charter: private aircraft, special-needs flights and SPACE TOURISM.
flashcards.answer:
• PRIVATE aircraft — symbolic market share; greater mobility/flexibility; company or individual owned.
• SPECIAL-NEEDS small-aircraft flights in a destination — panoramic (sightseeing), photography/filming/nature, sports/recreation (skydiving; + paragliding/hang-gliding without aircraft).
• SPACE TOURISM (since 2000): orbital, suborbital, lunar; first space tourist Dennis Tito (2001, ISS, ~$20 m); spaceflight's carbon footprint is ~100× a long-haul flight; demand exceeds supply despite high prices.
flashcards.explanation: Companies: Blue Origin (Bezos), Virgin Galactic (Branson) — suborbital tourist flights since July 2021.

quiz.question: The UNIQUE advantage of air transport is:
options: The largest passenger capacity of all modes

quiz.question: Air transport needs infrastructure built:
options: Only at the start/end points (airports); routes are imagined corridors

quiz.question: Low-cost carriers are NOT the same as charter because LCC:
options: Operate in the SCHEDULED system with a published flight schedule

quiz.question: Which charter type means exclusive use of the aircraft for the whole season (most economical)?
The airport-transfer problem means that:
options: Airports are always in the city centre
Getting to/from the airport can take longer than the flight itself
No other mode is ever needed

quiz.question: Low-cost carriers help create NEW tourist destinations mainly by:
options: Using only the largest hub airports
Choosing secondary/smaller airports and connecting smaller cities

quiz.question: Who is regarded as the first space tourist (2001, ISS)?

fillBlanks.sentence: Air transport needs infrastructure only at its start and end points, the _______.
Because it depends on fixed start/end points and needs road transfer, air transport is _______.
Low-cost carriers often fly from cheaper _______ airports.
Charter transport is based on a high aircraft _______ of 80–90%.
A _______ charter reserves the aircraft exclusively for the entire season and is the most economical.
Besides airplanes, historic rigid airships called _______ once carried transoceanic passengers.
Suborbital, orbital and lunar trips belong to _______ tourism.

learn.title: Air Transport (Connecting & Tourism Product)
learn.content:
Speed over distance

Air transport dominates intercontinental passenger and tourist flows. Its unbeatable edge is speed (~900 km/h) over long distances, with infrastructure needed only at the airports (routes are imagined corridors).

+ speed · long distance · no route infrastructure  |  − inelastic · airport-transfer problem · high fuel & cost · modest capacity (~500 pax)

Commercial air traffic

  • Line (scheduled): large traditional airlines vs low-cost carriers (LCC) — LCC cut cost via no frills, secondary airports, fast turnarounds, online sales, dynamic pricing; LCC ≠ charter; LCC carry ~30% of ~9 bn annual air passengers and create new destinations.
  • Charter: high occupancy (80–90%), lower quality/price, by contract (airline = transport, agency = sales). Types: whole · part/split · ad hoc · series · time (whole season, most economical).
  • Private aircraft, special-needs small-aircraft flights (panoramic, sports/skydiving) and space tourism (orbital/suborbital/lunar; first tourist Dennis Tito, 2001; ~100× the carbon footprint of a long-haul flight).

Air ≠ airplane only

Airplanes dominate, but balloons (economical, less safe) and historic zeppelins (transoceanic airships) are also air carriers. Airports are complex, expensive multimodal hubs near big cities — but far enough out that the transfer can take longer than a short flight.

flashcards.question: What is the role of MARITIME passenger transport today, and the SHIP's characteristics?
flashcards.answer:
Once the most important branch, maritime now has a MODEST share of passenger flows (its cargo role remains irreplaceable). Passenger maritime is limited to line service over shorter distances, round trips/excursions and personal-needs transport.

SHIP characteristics: large capacity; LOW speed; low transport costs; route flexibility (no route infrastructure); the second-safest means of transport (after rail).
flashcards.explanation: Like air, ships need no built route — only ports — but they are slow, so passenger use is mostly tourism/local lines.

flashcards.question: Compare HIGH-SPEED SHIPS and FERRIES.
flashcards.answer:
• HIGH-SPEED SHIPS (catamarans, hydrofoils) — light materials, gas-turbine/jet propulsion, high speeds; smaller one-time capacity → sail several times a day; economical only on high-constant-demand lines.
• FERRIES — carry passengers AND vehicles; need very SHORT port stays (organised like airports) for many turnovers = large 'dynamic' capacity; biggest ones resemble cruise ships (cabins, entertainment).
flashcards.explanation: Ferries trade comfort for throughput; high-speed ships trade capacity for speed.

flashcards.question: Describe maritime transport INFRASTRUCTURE (ports, terminals, marinas).
flashcards.answer:
Ports → specialised passenger TERMINALS (reception of ships & passengers, comfort, links to other modes). Types: terminals for regular line traffic; for round trips in territorial sea; for INTERNATIONAL cruises (near airport, police/customs, rich facilities). The key element is the WHARF (pier).

Also: MARINAS, sports ports & harbours (the basis of nautical tourism), and signalling/safety devices & waterways.
flashcards.explanation: International cruise terminals double as part of the tourist product — designed so waiting feels like part of the cruise.

flashcards.question: How is maritime transport ORGANISED, and what defines LINE passenger traffic?
flashcards.answer:
Organisation: (A) LINE traffic; (B) SPECIAL-NEEDS traffic (round trips & excursions — exclusively tourism); (C) PERSONAL-needs traffic.

LINE traffic runs by a sailing schedule (seasonal), maintained by a group of similar ships, operated by a liner shipping company — on high-demand lines (private/state) AND low-demand 'lines of special state interest' (state-subsidised, e.g. to sustain island life & tourism).
flashcards.explanation: State subsidies on unprofitable island lines keep both island life and island tourism possible.

flashcards.question: Contrast INTERNATIONAL CRUISES with cruises in territorial waters.
flashcards.answer:
• INTERNATIONAL cruises — huge CRUISE SHIPS (thousands of pax; largest ~7,600 on 'Icon of the Seas'), 20 decks, many facilities; profit via ECONOMIES OF SCALE; ~1/3 of passenger numbers are 'white staff'; tourist product = transport + on-board offer + ports visited.
• TERRITORIAL-water cruises — smaller ships (≤~150 pax), simpler organisation, smaller ports/destinations, offer built on local gastronomy, sea & nature.
flashcards.explanation: Cruise revenue is forecast in the tens of billions of USD; the most popular regions are the Caribbean and the Mediterranean.

flashcards.question: What is NAUTICAL TOURISM, and how is its transport function realised?
flashcards.answer:
Nautical tourism = sailing & staying in special vessels (boats/yachts, rented or owned) for recreation, sport and leisure — a tourism form based on the transport component of maritime transport. Needs accessible, indented, warm, moderate-climate coasts.

Transport function via: (a) PORT-NAUTICAL activity in MARINAS (infrastructure), and (b) RENTING/CHARTERING a vessel (daily, weekly, local, international charter).
flashcards.explanation: Marinas (commercial/club/sports) are the backbone; charter (with or without skipper) is the rental side.

flashcards.question: What characterises INLAND WATERWAY (river-lake-canal) transport in tourism?
flashcards.answer:
INLAND WATER = river + canal + lake traffic. Features: route inelasticity, low speed, high dependence on WEATHER & water level, unequal river characteristics, costly waterway maintenance.

Role in tourism is SMALL but with niches: river CRUISES (smaller ships, ~up to 400 pax, continuous bank views — chosen by those who fear rough seas) and EXCURSIONS/panoramic trips. Famous rivers: Nile, Rhine, Danube, Yangtze, Mississippi.
flashcards.explanation: River cruising suits travellers who want calm water and constant scenery rather than open-sea sailing.

quiz.question: In passenger flows today, maritime transport has:
options: A modest share, limited to lines, round trips/excursions and personal needs

quiz.question: A ferry differs from a high-speed ship mainly because it:
options: Carries passengers AND vehicles, with very short port stays for many turnovers

quiz.question: International cruise ships base their profitability on:
'Lines of special state interest' (subsidised maritime lines) exist mainly to:
options: Sustain island life and enable tourism where transport would otherwise be unprofitable

quiz.question: The backbone infrastructure of nautical tourism is the:
Compared with maritime cruises, river cruises typically have:
options: Far larger ships and rough water
Smaller ships, calm water and continuous bank views

quiz.question: The ship is described as the ____-safest means of transport.

fillBlanks.sentence: A ship that carries both passengers and vehicles, with very short port stays, is a _______.
International cruise ships earn profit mainly through economies of _______.
The key construction element of a passenger sea terminal is the _______ (pier).
The backbone of nautical-tourism infrastructure is the _______.
Renting a vessel with or without a skipper is a form of _______.
Unprofitable but socially vital island routes are lines of special _______ interest.
River, canal and lake traffic together form _______ waterway transport.

learn.title: Water Transport — Maritime & Inland Waterway
learn.content:
Slow, spacious, scenic

Water transport needs no built route (only ports), offers huge capacity and low cost, but is slow. The ship is the second-safest mode (after rail). In passenger flows its role is modest and largely touristic.

Maritime organisation: (A) LINE · (B) SPECIAL-NEEDS (round trips & excursions = tourism) · (C) PERSONAL
Vessels: high-speed ships (speed) · ferries (passengers + vehicles, throughput) · cruise ships (scale)

Cruises & nautical tourism

  • International cruises — giant ships (largest ~7,600 pax, 'Icon of the Seas'), profit via economies of scale; product = transport + on-board offer + ports (Caribbean & Mediterranean lead).
  • Territorial-water cruises — smaller ships, local gastronomy & nature.
  • Nautical tourism — sailing/staying in boats & yachts; realised through marinas (commercial/club/sports) + vessel charter (daily/weekly/local/ international).

Infrastructure & inland waterways

Ports become specialised terminals (the wharf/pier is the key element); international cruise terminals are part of the product. State-subsidised 'lines of special interest' sustain island life & tourism. Inland waterway (river-lake-canal) transport plays a small but niche role — river cruises (calm water, constant scenery) on the Nile, Rhine, Danube, Yangtze, Mississippi.

flashcards.question: What determines the VALUE of a transport service to a tourist?
flashcards.answer:
Value = the benefit the tourist gets (being moved, in comfort, safely, on time, with experience) WEIGHED against what they pay (price + time + effort).

Because transport demand is DERIVED, its value is judged by how well it serves the wider tourism purpose — reaching and enjoying the destination — not by the trip in isolation.
flashcards.explanation: This is syllabus learning-outcome 3: place the transport service's value & cost inside the tourism-product price.

flashcards.question: Which QUALITY dimensions define a good passenger transport service?
flashcards.explanation: Surveys show satisfaction is usually high for ticketing/info and lower for WiFi, complaint-handling and disabled assistance.

flashcards.question: How is the PRICE of a transport service built, and how does it sit in the tourism-product price?
flashcards.answer:
Carriers face large FIXED costs (vehicles, infrastructure, crew) and cannot store capacity, so price aims to maximise CAPACITY OCCUPANCY. Hence:
• DYNAMIC pricing (earlier/online = cheaper; price tracks supply/demand);
• the transport cost is then EMBEDDED in the final tourism-product price the tourist pays.
Transport is often a large share of total trip cost, so its price strongly moves tourism demand.
flashcards.explanation: Low-cost carriers and charter are essentially strategies to push occupancy up and unit price down.

flashcards.question: Why is achieving high CAPACITY OCCUPANCY the central economic problem of carriers?
flashcards.answer:
Because the transport service is PERISHABLE (an empty seat is lost forever) and costs are mostly FIXED. A carrier can barely change its fixed/variable costs in the short run, so profitability depends almost entirely on FILLING the capacity on each departure.

Tools: marketing & sales function, dynamic pricing, charter contracts, combining tourist with non-tourist flows.
flashcards.explanation: This is why an 'efficiently organised sales function' is described as essential for airlines and all carriers.

flashcards.question: How does QUALITY differ between, say, a charter flight and a scheduled flight, or a ferry and a cruise?
flashcards.explanation: There is no single 'best' quality — the right level depends on the market segment and the role transport plays in the product.

flashcards.question: What is the role of INFORMATION & passenger rights in transport-service quality?
flashcards.answer: Good, timely INFORMATION (timetables, connections, real-time delay info) and clear PASSENGER RIGHTS (compensation for delays, assistance for reduced mobility, easy complaints) are core quality components. The EU treats integrated information & ticketing and a journey's carbon-footprint info as emerging passenger rights.
flashcards.explanation: Information quality directly shapes perceived value — surveys rank it among the best-rated aspects, while complaint-handling lags.

quiz.question: The VALUE of a transport service to a tourist is judged mainly by:
options: How well it serves the wider tourism purpose, weighed against price/time/effort

quiz.question: The central economic problem of every carrier is to:
options: Maximise capacity occupancy on each departure (the service is perishable)

quiz.question: Dynamic pricing (earlier/online cheaper) exists chiefly to:
options: Fill capacity by tracking the supply–demand relationship

quiz.question: A charter flight typically offers, versus a scheduled flight:
options: Lower quality (comfort/times/airports) at a lower price and high occupancy

quiz.question: Which is a QUALITY dimension of passenger transport confirmed by EU surveys?
Within the tourism-product price, the transport cost is:
options: Embedded, and often a large share that strongly moves demand

learn.title: The Value & Quality of Transportation Services
learn.content:
What the tourist really pays for

The value of a transport service is the benefit (being moved comfortably, safely, on time, with experience) weighed against price, time and effort — and judged by how well it serves the wider tourism purpose (derived demand). This is syllabus learning-outcome 3.

Carrier economics: mostly FIXED costs + PERISHABLE service ⇒ goal = maximise CAPACITY OCCUPANCY
Transport cost ⇒ embedded in the tourism-product PRICE ⇒ strongly moves demand

Quality dimensions (from EU surveys)

  • Safety & feeling of safety · punctuality & reliability · price/value · comfort & cleanliness · frequency & availability · information (real-time/delays) · easy & integrated ticketing · accessibility & complaint handling.
  • Surveys rank ticketing & information highest; WiFi, complaint-handling and disabled assistance lag.

Price, occupancy & quality trade-offs

Because a seat is perishable and costs are fixed, carriers live or die by occupancy — hence dynamic pricing, charter and low-cost models, and an essential sales function. Quality is deliberately traded against price & purpose: charter = lower quality/price/high occupancy; scheduled = higher quality/price; ferry = throughput; cruise = the experience itself. Good information & passenger rights are core quality components.

flashcards.question: How is traffic SAFETY manifested and what does it include?
flashcards.answer:
Safety is manifested through: the number of traffic accidents, the number of dead & injured persons, and material damage.

It includes: the means of transport (freight & passenger), the persons who operate vehicles, and ALL road users. Increasing safety is a CONTINUOUS process and an important determinant of transport-service quality.
flashcards.explanation: Material damage value is not systematically tracked but is estimated at ~1–3% of GDP.

flashcards.question: Distinguish ACTIVE and PASSIVE vehicle safety, with examples.
flashcards.answer:
• ACTIVE safety = features that PREVENT accidents (mitigate the chance): brakes, steering, tyres, lights/signals, vision aids, seat construction, climate control, in-vehicle control/navigation.
• PASSIVE safety = features that REDUCE the damage once an accident happens: body & door construction, SEAT BELTS, headrests, windshields/mirrors, position of engine/tank/battery, bumpers, AIRBAGS.
flashcards.explanation: Mnemonic: ACTIVE = avoid the crash; PASSIVE = protect in the crash.

flashcards.question: What is the 'Safe System' / Vision Zero approach to road safety?
flashcards.answer: Vision Zero's 'Safe Systems Approach' is a PARADIGM SHIFT: ultimate responsibility for road safety moves FROM the individual road user TO those who design and run the transport system. Effort goes into designing roads & vehicles so that crashes do NOT lead to serious consequences — focusing on roads, vehicles and stakeholders, not just individual behaviour.
flashcards.explanation: Strategic frameworks: Valletta Declaration; EU Road Safety Policy Framework 2021–2030; EU target: halve road deaths and serious accidents.

flashcards.question: How do INFRASTRUCTURE and the HUMAN factor affect road safety?
flashcards.answer:
INFRASTRUCTURE: most fatal/serious accidents occur on unclassified roads; fewest on highways & local roads. Infrastructure alone is a factor in ~1% of serious accidents, but combined with a person in as much as ~35%.

HUMAN (driver): behaviour shaped by character/attitude, health condition, and education/culture. The driver is the most common culprit; pedestrians, cyclists and motorcyclists are most at risk.
flashcards.explanation: Almost 1 in 4 serious speed-related accidents is caused by drivers aged 25 or younger.

flashcards.question: Compare the SAFETY LEVEL across transport sectors.
flashcards.explanation: Road dominates fatalities because it carries the most traffic and is the least 'systemically' controlled.

flashcards.question: What are the key SAFETY features by sector (rail, air, maritime)?
flashcards.answer:
• RAIL — very safe (signalling & line control); fewer but sometimes severe accidents.
• AIR — safety from subsystem elements (communication/navigation, flight control, airports, aircraft) + security against unforeseen events (terrorism: passenger/baggage control, biometrics, explosive-detection dogs).
• MARITIME — passenger shipping adopted the ISM Code (safety procedures); risks: ferry construction (no transverse partitions), high-speed-ship behaviour in rough seas, high automation eroding manual skills.
flashcards.explanation: Each mode's safety system reflects its specific technology and risks.

flashcards.question: Why is traffic safety especially important FROM A TOURISM viewpoint?
flashcards.answer:
Because of the HIGH share of road traffic in tourist flows, tourists are exposed to accident risk — and fatalities/injuries in tourism-heavy countries PEAK during the tourist season.

Responses: information systems for road users (traffic/weather/route info to avoid jams & risky situations) and vehicle-monitoring systems (sensors warning the driver of unexpected behaviour).
flashcards.explanation: Seasonality of travel patterns is clearly visible in the seasonal distribution of road fatalities.

quiz.question: The 'Safe System' / Vision Zero approach shifts responsibility:
options: From the individual user toward those who design and run the transport system

options: Road (and air), which carry the most passengers

learn.title: Safety in Traffic
learn.content:
A determinant of transport quality

Traffic safety shows up in the number of accidents, casualties and material damage (~1–3% of GDP) and covers vehicles, operators and all road users. Improving it is a continuous process and a core part of transport-service quality.

ACTIVE safety = prevent the crash (brakes, steering, tyres, lights)
PASSIVE safety = reduce the damage (seat belts, airbags, body/door, headrests)

The three influences + Vision Zero

  • Vehicle (active + passive), infrastructure (worst on unclassified roads; a factor with a person in ~35% of serious crashes) and the human/driver (most common culprit; young drivers over-represented in speed crashes).
  • Vision Zero / Safe System — shift responsibility from the individual to system designers; frameworks: Valletta Declaration, EU Road Safety Policy 2021–2030; EU target: halve road deaths.

Safety by sector & in tourism

Safety is lowest in road (and air) — the busiest modes; rail & maritime are comparatively safe (rail ~1.8 deaths/million in 2022; road ~46/million in 2022). Air relies on subsystem safety + security (biometrics, screening); maritime on the ISM Code. From a tourism view, the heavy road share exposes tourists to risk, and fatalities peak in the tourist season — countered by traffic-information and vehicle-monitoring systems.

flashcards.question: How big is transport's environmental footprint in the EU?
flashcards.answer:
Transport is responsible for about a QUARTER (~25%) of the EU's total CO2/greenhouse-gas emissions. Of transport emissions, ~71.7% come from ROAD transport (2019).

Transport is the ONLY major sector where greenhouse-gas emissions have INCREASED over the past three decades.
flashcards.explanation: That 'only sector still rising' fact is why transport is the hardest, highest-priority part of EU climate policy.

flashcards.question: Within road transport, who are the biggest CO2 polluters?
flashcards.answer:
PASSENGER CARS are the major polluter — accounting for ~61% of total CO2 emissions from EU road transport. Road transport overall accounts for about a FIFTH of all EU emissions.

In 2019, most cars used diesel (~67%); electric cars were ~17.8% of newly registered passenger cars (rising fast since 2017).
flashcards.explanation: Because cars dominate both mobility AND emissions, decarbonising cars is the single biggest lever.

flashcards.question: What negative external (environmental) effects does transport cause?
flashcards.explanation: Internalising these costs — making users pay — is a central EU instrument ('polluter pays').

flashcards.question: How do transport MODES compare environmentally?
flashcards.answer:
RAIL is the greenest motorised mode (electric drive, little land use, high efficiency — high-speed rail is ~9× more efficient than flying). WATER is efficient per tonne but slow. ROAD (esp. cars) and AIR are the most carbon-intensive per passenger.

EU policy therefore pushes a MODAL SHIFT from road & air toward rail, public transport, cycling and walking.
flashcards.explanation: Active modes (walking, cycling) and electrified rail are the backbone of 'green mobility'.

flashcards.question: Are ELECTRIC cars really cleaner?
flashcards.answer:
Two ways to cut car CO2: make vehicles more efficient OR change the fuel. Production & disposal of an EV is LESS environmentally friendly than a combustion car, and EV emissions depend on how the electricity is produced.

HOWEVER, using the average European energy mix, EVs are ALREADY cleaner than petrol cars — and will get cleaner as renewable electricity grows.
flashcards.explanation: Whole-life-cycle thinking matters: count production, use AND disposal, not just tailpipe emissions.

flashcards.question: What EU measures target transport emissions?
flashcards.explanation: These tie directly into the Green Deal goal of −90% transport emissions by 2050 (next topic).

learn.title: Ecological Aspects of Transport
learn.content:
Transport's environmental problem

Transport causes about a quarter of EU greenhouse-gas emissions, ~71.7% of them from road. Crucially, it is the only major sector where emissions have risen over three decades — making it the hardest part of EU climate policy.

Transport ≈ 25% of EU GHG · road ≈ 71.7% of transport emissions · cars ≈ 61% of road CO2
Greenest motorised mode = RAIL · dirtiest per passenger = car & air

External effects & the modal hierarchy

  • External effects: CO2 & air pollution, noise, water pollution (tyre microplastics), habitat loss, congestion — borne by society ('external costs').
  • Modal comparison: rail (electric, efficient) is greenest; push a modal shift from road/air to rail, public transport, cycling & walking.
  • Electric cars: dirtier to make/dispose, but with the EU energy mix already cleaner than petrol — and improving as renewables grow (think whole life-cycle).

What the EU is doing

Zero-CO2 new cars by 2035 (−55% by 2030; effective petrol/diesel ban); Emissions Trading extended to road, maritime & revised for aviation; more renewable fuels; end of fossil-fuel tax breaks; 'polluter pays' / 'user pays' internalisation. All feed the Green Deal target of −90% transport emissions by 2050 (see 'Future of transport').

flashcards.question: What is the EU 'Sustainable and Smart Mobility Strategy' (2020) and its headline goal?
flashcards.answer:
It is the EU Commission's roadmap (COM(2020) 789) to put European transport 'on track for the future' — sustainable, smart and resilient. It identifies 10 FLAGSHIP areas.

Headline goal (Green Deal): a 90% REDUCTION in transport emissions by 2050, on the way to a climate-neutral EU by 2050.
flashcards.explanation: Context: transport = ~5% of EU GDP, ~10 million jobs, but ~25% of EU emissions.

flashcards.question: What are the THREE pillars of the future strategy?
flashcards.explanation: Pillar 1 = cleaner vehicles; Pillar 2 = modal shift & multimodality; Pillar 3 = get the prices right.

flashcards.question: Name key MILESTONES of the strategy (2030 / 2035 / 2050).
flashcards.answer:
By 2030: ≥30 million zero-emission cars on the roads; 100 climate-neutral cities; HIGH-SPEED RAIL traffic DOUBLED; scheduled collective travel <500 km carbon-neutral; large-scale automated mobility; zero-emission vessels market-ready.
By 2035: zero-emission large AIRCRAFT market-ready.
By 2050: nearly all cars/vans/buses & new heavy vehicles zero-emission; rail freight DOUBLED; high-speed rail TRIPLED; TEN-T fully operational.
flashcards.explanation: Notice the central role of rail (double by 2030, triple by 2050) — the modal-shift backbone.

flashcards.question: What does 'SMART' mobility mean (digital/automated future)?
flashcards.explanation: 'Smart' complements 'sustainable': digital tools make the green, multimodal system actually work.

flashcards.question: What is MULTIMODALITY and 'Mobility as a Service' (MaaS) in the future system?
flashcards.answer:
MULTIMODALITY combines the strengths of different modes (speed, cost, reliability) into one efficient journey. MaaS integrates many transport services into one on-demand, digitally accessible service — ideally one SINGLE integrated ticket for a door-to-door, multimodal trip.

Goal: by 2030, seamless multimodal passenger transport via integrated electronic ticketing; paperless freight.
flashcards.explanation: This is exactly the 'single ticket for all modes' that citizens rated most useful (K1, Mobility patterns).

flashcards.question: Give a real example showing how better transport SHIFTS demand toward sustainable modes.
flashcards.answer:
After the Barcelona–Madrid HIGH-SPEED RAIL line opened, the air/rail modal split on that route changed from ~85% plane / 15% train (2008) to ~38% air / 62% rail (2016).

Also: external (environmental) costs of EU transport are ~€388 billion per year — which 'polluter pays' pricing aims to internalise.
flashcards.explanation: When a fast, affordable green alternative exists, travellers switch — proof that infrastructure + pricing can drive the transition.

flashcards.question: What does 'RESILIENT' mobility mean, and why did COVID-19 highlight it?
flashcards.answer:
Resilient mobility = a transport system that keeps functioning through crises (pandemics, energy shocks, supply disruptions). COVID-19 caused steep falls in travel/tourism and severe difficulties for transport SMEs, showing how vital a well-functioning single market and connectivity are.

The strategy aims to help transport — and tourism — 'build back better': greener, smarter, more resilient.
flashcards.explanation: Resilience joins 'sustainable' and 'smart' as the third quality of future EU mobility.

learn.title: The Future of Transport
learn.content:
Sustainable · Smart · Resilient

The EU Sustainable and Smart Mobility Strategy (2020, COM(2020) 789) is the roadmap for European transport, organised around 10 flagships. Headline goal: a 90% cut in transport emissions by 2050 (transport = ~5% of GDP, ~10 m jobs, but ~25% of emissions).

THREE PILLARS: (1) cleaner modes & fuels · (2) sustainable alternatives in a MULTIMODAL system · (3) right INCENTIVES (carbon pricing, 'polluter pays')

Milestones

  • 2030: ≥30 m zero-emission cars · 100 climate-neutral cities · HSR doubled · collective travel <500 km carbon-neutral · large-scale automated mobility.
  • 2035: zero-emission large aircraft market-ready.
  • 2050: nearly all road vehicles zero-emission · rail freight doubled · HSR tripled · TEN-T complete.

Smart & resilient

Smart: connected/automated mobility (CCAM), Mobility as a Service (one integrated ticket), AI, 5G, a Common Mobility Data Space, ERTMS (rail) & Single European Sky (air), drones. Resilient: a system that survives crises — COVID-19 showed how vital connectivity is for transport and tourism. Proof it works: after Barcelona–Madrid HSR opened, the air/rail split moved from 85/15 (2008) to 38/62 in favour of rail (2016); EU transport's external costs (~€388 bn/yr) are what pricing aims to internalise.
